33:5/ailis-door.2.text: I'll tell you one thing and then you'll go.

33:6.2.1.text: That pack. Where'd you get that?

33:6.2.2.text: Hm. Leeches are in the tank. Crawlers in the cooler. Coffee's a dollar, nobody pays it.

33:6.2.3.text: You have his tent. Is it holding up?

33:6.2.4.text: Good. It should. He reproofed it every spring on the clothesline and swore at it. Coffee? There's bars. Sit. I'm not going to talk about him, but sit.

33:6.2.5.text: You know whose, or you wouldn't be standing in my bait shop with it.

33:6.2.c4.text: I found his notebook in it.

33:6.2.6.text: Don't. Whatever's in it, don't tell me. If I don't see it, I don't know it. Coffee? There's bars. Sit.

33:6.2.7.text: They found his canoe. That's what there is.

33:6.2.8.text: He went out at night from the bunkhouse on Moose Lake, and they found his canoe on Birch. Swamped. No paddle. That's what the sheriff said and that's what I say.

33:6.2.c7.text: I'm trying to find out what happened.

33:6.2.9.text: Lots of people have tried to find out what happened. They came here first, mostly. I made them coffee too.

33:6.2.10.text: People. Reporters. A man from the sheriff once. A man who said he was a friend of the family. We don't have friends of the family. We have family.

33:6.2.c9.text: Do you have anything of his?

33:6.2.11.text: I don't have anything of his.

33:6.2.12.text: They offered me his things after the service. The box you've got there, I suppose. I said no.

33:6.2.13.text: Because I didn't want it in the house.

33:6.2.14.text: Finish your coffee first. It's a long way back to anywhere from here.

33:6.2.17.text: Mm. They found his canoe. That's what there is. Leeches or crawlers?

33:6.3.1.text: My brothers and me. Basswood, our grandmother's place. Mummo's, we called it. That's the swimming rock.

33:6.3.2.text: The one holding me so I won't go in. The other one's already going in.

33:6.3.3.text: The government bought it when I was twelve. We burned the cabin on the ice ourselves, in February, so we wouldn't have to watch somebody else do it. There were lilacs. I suppose there still are. I've never been back.

33:6.3.4.text: Because it's a long way and I'd cry and there'd be Iowans.

33:6.3.c5.if: only if the player has read N02 or N03

33:6.3.5.text: His wife. She taught school in Tower. She was the only person who could make him stop talking about wind.

33:6.3.6.text: The blue one. He lost it off a rock somewhere. She laughed about it for a week. He didn't.

33:6.3.7.text: My husband. His folks had a camp up the lake before they bought everybody out. They came down to Crane with a boat and a bait tank and I married into the bait tank.

33:6.3.8.text: 2012. In the spring, at the kitchen table, with the radio on. The walleye opener was the next week and Jon went out and took his clients anyway. That's what you do.

33:6.3.9.text: Pekka's dad ran whiskey when he was sixteen. Canada to Loon Lake, over the Beatty, down the Indian Sioux. He said the worst part wasn't the law, it was the bugs. They had a hole somewhere past the river with a lid on it. He'd go quiet about where.

33:6.3.10.text: Some lake with the right name, he said, which I always thought was a joke. Ask Orrin Gilbertson. He buys that sort of thing. He's in cabin four all summer pretending to fish.

33:6.3.c11.if: After the player has been here at night once, or read NF1.

33:6.3.11.text: It's a motel. People come in late.

33:6.3.12.text: People come in late every night.

33:6.3.13.text: Keep them cool and don't let anybody tell you they need feeding.

33:6.3.c14.if: she never asks this; if the player volunteers a lake

33:6.3.14.text: Don't tell me where you're going. I don't want to know where.

33:6.4.1.text: They're still there. He loves those. Mummo put them in the year he was born— Loved. He loved those.

33:6.4.2.text: I'll tell you one thing and then you'll go. He always put a white stone on the stump where he landed. Our dad did that. Go.

33:6.4.3.text: It means he'd be back. Go. I'll see you next time.

33:6.4.5.text: June gave him that pot. Christmas, '84. He said a coffee pot was a rotten present and used it every day for four years and lost it off a rock.

33:6.4.6.text: I'll tell you one thing and then you'll go. He always put a white stone on the stump where he landed. Our dad did that. Go.

33:6.4.7.text: I'll keep coffee in it. That's what it's for.

33:6.4.c4.text: I'd like to cook with it.

33:6.4.8.text: Good. Somebody should. Don't lose it off a rock.

33:6.4.9.text: You keep going places for us. Stop it. Sit.

33:6.5.1.text: Nobody's said his name in here in a long time.

33:6.5.2.text: Wednesday the twelfth of October. I was twenty-five, still at home. He told Ma he was going for ducks on Bald Eagle. I went out to the porch for the milk at six and his shotgun was on the hooks.

33:6.5.c2.text: No gun for a duck hunt.

33:6.5.3.text: No gun for a duck hunt. I stood there with the milk.

33:6.5.4.text: The night before, he said Friday he was going to Duluth to see a man at the paper. He said it like it was a job interview. He said don't tell Ma.

33:6.5.5.text: No. I never told Ma anything after that. It was the only thing I could still do for him.

33:6.5.6.text: I told Walt about the gun. Walt said leave it. So I left it. Forty-nine years.

33:6.5.c6.text: Do you think somebody killed him?

33:6.5.7.text: I think he didn't take his gun. And I think he swam better than Walt, and everybody says that like it's a joke, and it isn't.

33:6.5.8.text: A month before, a man from the office came to the house. He sat in Ma's kitchen for an hour with his hat on his knee and talked about the weather. Ma made him coffee. I sat there. When he left, Ma washed his cup twice.

33:6.5.9.text: Sorensen. From the office. He's dead now. Ma never made anybody coffee in that cup again.

33:6.5.10.text: He didn't say what he wanted. That's how you knew.

33:6.5.11.text: So you'll forgive me. When a stranger comes in and talks about the weather.

33:6.5.12.text: That's all I'm going to say about that today. More coffee?

33:6.6.c2.text: Did a man named Helstrom come to the memorial?

33:6.6.1.text: Ninth of November, at the Lutheran in Ely. Everybody he ever guided came, it felt like. And men nobody knew. Nice coats. Shook my hand like they were sorry for something else.

33:6.6.2.text: That one wrote his name. Most of them didn't bother.

33:6.6.4.text: Then you don't need me to tell you anything.

33:6.6.5.text: Take it. I don't want it in the house either.

33:6.7.1.text: My mother's had enough people at the door. You're one more.

33:6.7.c1.text: I'm not here to bother her.

33:6.7.2.text: Everybody's not here to bother her.

33:6.7.c2.text: Did you know your uncle well?

33:6.7.3.text: Well enough to know you didn't.

33:6.7.4.text: Eaters. Sand Point, the bar off the second island, if it's out of the south. Don't tell anybody I said.

33:6.7.5.text: Go on. You're in my light.

33:6.7.c4.text: That was you on Sand Point.

33:6.7.6.text: I was on Crane all day with two guys from Des Moines. And {site} has no shade. You'll have cooked.
33:6.7.6.if: tell: the player never told him where they camped. If they shook him, the template is instead: "That island you sat behind is all rock. Must've been boring."

33:6.7.8.when: If they shook him in the islands, one more line

33:6.7.9.text: Wind's coming round to the north tomorrow. Whatever you're doing, do it early.

33:6.8.c2.text: One of his friends sold him.

33:6.8.1.text: That's his hand. He made his sevens with a bar through them. Army. 'Phone at 6.' Who called him?

33:6.8.3.text: Denny. Denny sent me a birthday card every year till I was twelve. Five dollars in it. I'm not going to do anything. I'm going to think about it for a long time.

33:6.8.4.text: Find out. Then don't tell me, or I'll do something.

33:6.8.5.text: Yeah. I saw. He meant you, I guess. Not us. He'd have known it'd be some stranger.

33:6.8.6.text: One of the boys. Mom fed those guys. Every one of them, in that kitchen, the year Walt turned sixty.

33:6.8.7.if: then as in A's Denny line

33:6.8.8.text: Yeah. It was me on Sand Point. Somebody had to see who you were.

33:6.8.9.text: Wasn't me you needed to worry about out there. Rented boat out of Crane, two guys, no rods, sat behind the island all day. And their buddy stood on the public dock at Crane the whole afternoon with a radio. Nice jacket. Fella never wet his boots.

33:6.8.10.text: The boat, three times since you showed up. The dock guy, once. That first winter after the canoe, there was a car went past the motel at seven and at five, every day. Mom's mail came late all winter. Then in spring it didn't.

33:6.8.11.text: I think my mother leaves the porch light on. That's all I think.

33:6.8.12.text: We don't talk about it. That's how we talk about it.

33:6.8.13.text: Because I didn't know what you were. I still don't. But you're not that.

33:6.8.14.text: When you go out of here, tell Liisa at the counter which day. Not where. Which day. If there's a truck at the landing that shouldn't be, I'll know.
33:6.8.14.if: After Liisa's season ends, the keeper takes the day instead: "Jon says tell him the day. Just the day."

33:6.8.15.text: {lake}. Go early. It blows up there after two.

33:6.8.16.text: People find all kinds of things over there. It's a big country.

33:6.8.17.text: Sauna's hot at eight. Mom won't come. She says it's for Finns who can't sit still.
33:6.8.17.if: a warm close, optional, any Saturday after 6.8

33:6.8.18.text: Löyly. He'd throw a whole dipper and laugh at me.

33:6.9.1.text: Hi. Are you the one with Uncle Walt's tent? Grandma came home and washed every cup in the motel. That's how I knew something happened.

33:6.9.2.text: Christmases. He brought smoked fish and fell asleep in Grandpa's chair and let me win at cribbage so badly I could tell. I was fifteen when he... when the canoe.

33:6.9.3.text: Grandma says he drowned. Grandma also keeps Christmas cards in a coffee can, so.

33:6.9.4.text: Never mind. I'm not supposed to be weird about it at the counter. Do you need a shuttle or not?

33:6.9.5.text: I was hoping you'd tell me. Nobody tells me anything. They just get quiet in a really specific way.

33:6.9.c5.text: Tell her one of his stories.

33:6.9.c6.text: It's in his notebook. His hand.

33:6.9.7.text: That's so him. He wrote like a weather report.

33:6.9.8.text: Can I... no. Keep it. I'd just want it.

33:6.9.10.text: He poured it in the lake? That's the saddest thing I've ever heard. Grandma does that with the dish soap. Uses two squirts and then pours one back.

33:6.9.11.text: June's pot! Grandma has a picture of it. It's blue. He lost it? That's so funny. Don't tell her I laughed.

33:6.9.12.text: Sparky. Who was Sparky? I bet it was the electrician. It's always the electrician.

33:6.9.13.text: He slept in a canoe? On purpose? That's either really cool or something's wrong with our family.

33:6.9.14.text: He'd hate that they're going to take it. He hated when people tidied things.

33:6.9.15.text: Gene was the nice one. He always had butterscotch.

33:6.9.16.text: He wrote about the porch light? She leaves it on every night. Dad says the electric bill's a crime.

33:6.9.17.text: Not today. Grandma goes to Cook on Mondays. Come back Monday.

33:6.9.18.text: Okay. You showed me something. I'll show you something.

33:6.9.19.text: There's never any writing. Just the little drawing. A stone on a stump. Every year.

33:6.9.20.text: A friend of Grandma's from before, I think. She keeps the envelopes. She never keeps envelopes. She throws out the electric bill envelope before she's read the bill.

33:6.9.21.text: The Christmas after... the year after the canoe. So 2020. One every year.

33:6.9.22.text: Yeah, but I have to go back, there's a party of eight from Wisconsin and only me. Put it back behind the boots before four. Please. She'll know if it's crooked.

33:6.10.1.text: You don't know anything. Drink your coffee.

33:6.10.2.text: She wasn't mad at me. She was mad at you. I don't get it. Grandma says I'm not to show anybody anything ever again. I wasn't showing you anything. I was showing you cards.

33:6.11.1.text: Dad says tell you there's a grey pickup at the public landing since six. Nobody's fished out of it. He said you'd know what that means. I don't, and I'd like to.

33:6.11.2.text: Truck at the landing. Same as yesterday. Go out the back way, through the narrows, and come in late.

33:6.11.3.text: Saw you got across all right.

33:6.12.1.text: A dozen's plenty. Lot of country up here. Easy to get turned around.
33:6.12.1.if: to Aili; to the player, pleasantly, as he passes

33:6.12.2.text: He's been in before. Leeches or crawlers?
33:6.12.2.if: if step 1 or higher; if step 0

33:6.13.1.text: You're a long way from your car, eh.

33:6.13.2.text: This was a mine town too. They closed around '80. We know how that goes. Now we sell you folks the lakes the mines didn't want.

33:6.13.3.text: They come up and buy our camps. Always have. Pay too much and leave in September and complain about the road.

33:6.13.4.text: An old fella came through a few falls back. American. Paid cash for a winter camp. Didn't fish. I noticed.

33:6.13.5.text: Quiet. Knew how to sit in a boat. He said thank you twice. Americans say it once. Finns say it twice.

33:6.13.c5.text: How do you know he was a Finn?

33:6.13.6.text: I don't. I know he said thank you twice.

33:6.13.7.text: North. People up there like being left alone. I'm the same, on Thursdays.

33:6.13.8.text: Didn't give one I'd remember. Cash doesn't have a name. That's why people like it.

33:6.13.c8.text: Gord said an old American bought a camp up there.

33:6.13.9.text: Gord talks. Thursdays he talks. I don't.

33:6.14.2.text: Good. Now I can tell them yes and mean it.

33:8/to-the-other-arcs.1.text: Yes. Well. He didn't go back.

33:9/the-journalist-walt-kept.1.text: They put your outfitter's name in the paper. Not yours. That was decent of somebody.

33:9/the-journalist-walt-kept.2.text: Mom turned the radio up for the news. She never turns the radio up.

33:9/the-journalist-walt-kept.3.text: Grandma put this one on the fridge. With a magnet. I don't know what that means but it's new.

33:9/the-journalist-walt-named.1.text: You knew. And you said it anyway.

33:9/the-journalist-walt-named.2.text: There were reporters from the Cities in the lot this morning. Then more. Mom put the closed sign up. First time since Dad died.

33:9/the-journalist-walt-named.3.text: Grandma burned the old cards in the stove the day it was in the paper. Like the cabin, she said. I don't know what cabin. This one came anyway.

33:9/the-companys-money-7.1.text: We've said what we have to say.

33:9/the-companys-money-7.2.text: Truck's gone from the landing. I guess you bought that.

33:9/the-companys-money-7.c1.text: It kept them away from you.

33:9/the-companys-money-7.3.text: Yeah. It did. Don't come down to the dock any more.

33:9/the-companys-money-7.4.text: I'm not supposed to talk to you. Sorry. You want a shuttle, it's forty dollars.

33:9/coda-the-postcard-on.2.text: I don't want to see it.

33:9/coda-the-postcard-on.3.text: We've said what we have to say.
